relationship: explicit quotation and fulfillment
rationale: Matthew expressly introduces Isaiah's words as fulfilled when Jesus settles in Galilee, repeating the great light for people in darkness and death's shadow.
source_text: You people who walk in darkness, behold a great light; you who dwell in a land and shadow of death, a light will shine upon you.

target_units.text: so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled:
“Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations:
the people sitting in darkness saw a great light, and for those sitting in the region and shadow of death a light rose.”

relationship: shared harvest image for joy
rationale: Isaiah compares the people's rejoicing with joy at harvest; the psalm likewise pictures reapers returning with exultation and their sheaves.
source_text: The multitude of the people whom Thou hast brought down in Thy gladness, they will rejoice before Thee, as people rejoice at harvest, and as those who divide the spoils.

target_units.text: Those sowing in tears will reap with exultation.
Going, they went and wept, carrying their seeds; but coming, they will arrive with exultation, carrying their sheaves.

relationship: shared spoil image for rejoicing
rationale: Isaiah also compares gladness with dividing spoils; the psalm compares joy in God's sayings with finding much spoil. The occasions of joy differ.
source_text: The multitude of the people whom Thou hast brought down in Thy gladness, they will rejoice before Thee, as people rejoice at harvest, and as those who divide the spoils.

target_units.text: I will rejoice in Thy sayings like one who finds much spoil.

relationship: explicit historical comparison with Midian's defeat
rationale: Isaiah names the day against Midian as the pattern for breaking oppression; Judges records the Lord turning Midian's camp against itself and Israel's pursuit of its rulers.
source_text: For the yoke laid upon them has been taken away, and the rod upon their neck; for the Lord has shattered the rod of their oppressors, as in the day against Midian.

target_units.text: The three companies sounded the horn trumpets and shattered the jars. They grasped the torches in their left hands, with the horn trumpets in their right hands to sound them, and cried, “A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!”
Each stood by himself around the camp. The whole camp ran; they sounded the alarm and fled.

The three hundred horn trumpets sounded, and the Lord set each man’s sword against his neighbour throughout the camp. The camp fled as far as Beth-shittah and, gathered together, as far as the edge of Abel-meholah and toward Tabbath.
The men of Israel cried out from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh, and they pursued Midian.

Gideon sent messengers throughout Ephraim’s territory, saying, “Go down to meet Midian and seize for yourselves the water as far as Beth-barah, and the Jordan.” All the men of Ephraim cried out, and they seized the water beforehand as far as Beth-barah, and the Jordan.
They captured Midian’s two rulers, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb in Sourin and Zeeb in Jakephzeeb, and pursued Midian. They brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon from beyond the Jordan.

relationship: legal counterpart of restitution for wrongfully acquired property
rationale: Isaiah requires restitution concerning robes gathered by deceit; Exodus includes a disputed garment among property for which the convicted wrongdoer must repay double. The fire wish is additional in Isaiah.
source_text: For every robe gathered by deceit, and every garment, they will repay with restitution; and they will wish that they had been burned with fire.

target_units.text: In every alleged wrong concerning a calf, beast of burden, sheep, garment, or any disputed loss, whatever it may be, the case of both parties shall come before God. Whoever is convicted through God shall repay his neighbour double.

relationship: related birth announcement joined with peace
rationale: Both join the birth of a child with an announcement of peace. Luke names the newborn Savior, Christ the Lord; Isaiah calls the child Messenger of Great Counsel.
source_text: For a child was born to us, a son also was given to us, whose rule was laid upon his shoulder; and his name is called Messenger of Great Counsel. For I will bring peace upon the rulers, peace and health to him.

target_units.text: today in David’s city a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord.
This is the sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.”
Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying,
“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of His favour.”

relationship: close Davidic throne and unending reign
rationale: Isaiah promises enduring rule upon David's throne; the angel likewise promises Jesus David's throne and a kingdom without end.
source_text: Great is his rule, and his peace has no limit, upon the throne of David and his kingdom, to establish it and uphold it in righteousness and judgment, from now on and for ever. The zeal of the Lord Sabaoth will do these things.

target_units.text: He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David,
and He will reign over Jacob’s house forever, and His kingdom will have no end.”

relationship: parallel royal righteousness, judgment and abundant peace
rationale: Isaiah joins the ruler's lasting peace with righteousness and judgment; the psalm likewise petitions for a king's righteous judgment, enduring life and abundant peace.
source_text: Great is his rule, and his peace has no limit, upon the throne of David and his kingdom, to establish it and uphold it in righteousness and judgment, from now on and for ever. The zeal of the Lord Sabaoth will do these things.

target_units.text: For Solomon. God, give Thy judgment to the king, and Thy righteousness to the king’s son,
to judge Thy people in righteousness, and Thy poor in justice.
Let the mountains take up peace for Thy people, and the hills in righteousness.
He will judge the poor of the people, and save the children of the needy, and humble the false accuser,
and he will endure alongside the sun, and before the moon, through generations of generations.
And he will descend like rain upon a fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth.
Righteousness will arise in his days, and abundant peace until the moon is taken away.

relationship: close divine sending of death upon Israel
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord sent death against Jacob and Israel; Amos likewise has God declare that He sent death among His people.
source_text: The Lord sent death against Jacob, and it came upon Israel,

target_units.text: “I sent death among you on Egypt’s road and killed your young men with the sword, along with the captivity of your horses. I brought your camps up in fire in My anger; yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

relationship: parallel judgment of Ephraim and Jacob's arrogance
rationale: Isaiah introduces Ephraim and Samaria's insolent, lofty speech; Amos announces Ephraim's captivity and God's abhorrence of Jacob's arrogance.
source_text: and all Ephraim’s people and those settled in Samaria will know, saying in insolence and a lofty heart,

target_units.text: Therefore now they will be captives from the foremost of the powerful, and horses’ neighing will be removed from Ephraim.
For the Lord swore by Himself: “I abhor all Jacob’s arrogance and have hated his regions; I will remove the city with all who inhabit it.”

relationship: related collective tower-building boast with bricks and stone
rationale: Isaiah's speakers propose hewn stones and a tower after bricks fall; Genesis likewise records a collective tower-building proposal using brick for stone and seeking a name. The construction details differ.
source_text: “Bricks have fallen, but come, let us hew stones, cut down sycamores and cedars, and build ourselves a tower.”

target_units.text: And each said to his neighbour, “Come, let us make bricks and burn them in the fire.” And they used brick for stone, and pitch for mortar.
And they said, “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose summit shall reach unto heaven, and let us make a name for ourselves before we are scattered over the face of the whole earth.”

relationship: close devouring of Israel by foreign nations
rationale: Isaiah pictures Syria and the Greeks devouring Israel; the psalm says nations devoured Jacob and desolated his place. The psalm leaves those nations unnamed.
source_text: Syria from the sun’s rising and the Greeks from the sun’s setting, who devour Israel with their whole mouth. For all these things the anger did not turn away, but the hand is still high.

target_units.text: Pour out Thy wrath upon nations that do not know Thee, and upon kingdoms that did not call on Thy name,
for they devoured Jacob and made his place desolate.

relationship: related divine blows and failure to turn toward God
rationale: Isaiah says the people did not turn back until struck and did not seek the Lord; Amos joins divine blows with the repeated statement that Israel still did not turn to Him. Their stated timing differs.
source_text: The people did not turn back until they were struck, and they did not seek the Lord.

target_units.text: “I struck you with burning and jaundice. You multiplied your gardens; the caterpillar devoured your vineyards, fig orchards and olive groves, yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

“I sent death among you on Egypt’s road and killed your young men with the sword, along with the captivity of your horses. I brought your camps up in fire in My anger; yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

relationship: same-chapter explanation of head and tail
rationale: The removal of Israel's head and tail is immediately explained by identifying leadership with the elder and those showing favoritism, and the tail with the prophet teaching lawless things.
source_text: The Lord removed from Israel head and tail, great and small, in one day,

target_units.text: the elder and those who show favoritism—this is the leadership—and the prophet teaching lawless things—this is the tail.

relationship: parallel condemnation of lawless prophets
rationale: Isaiah identifies a prophet teaching lawlessness as the tail; Jeremiah likewise condemns Samaria's prophets for misleading Israel and Jerusalem's prophets for supporting evil conduct.
source_text: the elder and those who show favoritism—this is the leadership—and the prophet teaching lawless things—this is the tail.

target_units.text: And among Samaria’s prophets I saw lawless acts: they prophesied through Baal and led My people Israel astray.

And among Jerusalem’s prophets I have seen horrifying things: committing adultery, walking in lies, and supporting evil hands so that no one turns from his evil way. They all became like Sodom to Me, and her inhabitants like Gomorrah.

relationship: close misleading assurances given to the disobedient
rationale: Isaiah says those blessing the people lead them astray; Jeremiah warns against prophets who promise peace and freedom from evils to those rejecting God's word.
source_text: Those blessing this people will lead astray, and they lead astray in order to swallow them up.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Do not listen to the prophets’ words, because they make a vision futile for themselves. They speak from their own heart and not from the Lord’s mouth.

They say to those rejecting the Lord’s word, You will have peace. To all who walk according to their own wishes, to everyone walking in the wandering of his heart, they said, No evils will come upon you.

relationship: parallel withholding of pity in comprehensive judgment
rationale: Isaiah denies pity even to orphans and widows amid general lawlessness; Jeremiah similarly denies sparing or pitying a people whose rulers, families, priests and prophets face destruction. The named groups differ.
source_text: Therefore God will not rejoice over their young men, and He will not pity their orphans or widows, because all are lawless and evil, and every mouth speaks unjust things. For all these things the anger did not turn away, but the hand is still high.

target_units.text: then you will say to them: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am filling those dwelling in this land, and their kings, David’s sons who sit on his throne, and the priests and prophets and Judah and all those dwelling in Jerusalem, with intoxication,
and I will scatter them, a man and his brother, their fathers and their sons together. I will not yearn for them, says the Lord, nor spare nor pity them so as to withhold their destruction.

relationship: shared forest-fire image for destructive unrighteousness
rationale: Isaiah likens lawlessness to fire consuming thickets; James likens the unrighteous tongue to a small fire setting a great forest ablaze.
source_text: Lawlessness will burn like fire and be consumed by fire like dry grass; it will burn in the forest’s thickets and consume together everything around the hills.

target_units.text: So also the tongue is a small member and boasts great things. Look how small a fire sets so great a forest ablaze!
And the tongue is a fire. The tongue is established among our members as a world of unrighteousness, staining the whole body, setting the wheel of life ablaze, and itself set ablaze by Gehenna.

relationship: parallel divine anger consuming like fire
rationale: Isaiah describes the earth and people burned through the Lord's fury; Jeremiah warns that His anger will kindle an unquenchable fire consuming the woodland and its surroundings. The stated extent differs.
source_text: Through the fury of the Lord’s anger the whole earth has been burned, and the people will be as though burned by fire. A person will not pity his brother,

target_units.text: House of David, thus says the Lord: Judge a judgment in the morning, set things straight, and rescue the plundered from the hand of the one wronging him, so that My anger is not kindled like fire and burns with no one to quench it.
Behold, I am against you who dwell in the valley of Sor, the level land, you who say, Who will frighten us? Or who will enter our dwelling?
And I will kindle a fire in her woodland, and it will consume everything around her.

relationship: related hunger expressed through eating human flesh
rationale: Isaiah describes hunger unrelieved by eating one's own arm; Deuteronomy warns that besieged people will eat their children's flesh. The flesh and circumstances are specified differently.
source_text: but will turn to the right because he will hunger, and eat from the left; a person eating the flesh of his own arm will certainly not be filled.

target_units.text: And you shall eat the offspring of your womb, the flesh of your sons and of your daughters whom the Lord your God has given you, in your straitness and in your distress wherewith your enemy shall afflict you.
The tender and most delicate man among you shall look grudgingly upon his brother, and the wife of his bosom, and the children who remain unto him,
begrudging any of them the flesh of his children which he eats, because nothing is left unto him, in your straitness and in your distress wherewith your enemies shall afflict you in all your cities.

relationship: shared mutual-devouring image for communal hostility
rationale: Isaiah portrays Manasseh and Ephraim eating from one another; Paul warns a community biting and devouring one another that mutual consumption may result. Isaiah specifically names Israelite tribes.
source_text: For Manasseh will eat from Ephraim, and Ephraim from Manasseh, because together they will besiege Judah. For all these things the anger did not turn away, but the hand is still high.

target_units.text: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.

relationship: parallel injustice exercised through authoritative commands
rationale: Isaiah condemns writing wickedness, explained in 10:2 as denying justice; the psalm likewise describes a lawless throne shaping toil by command and condemning innocent blood.
source_text: Woe to those writing wickedness! For when they write, they write wickedness,

target_units.text: Will a throne of lawlessness join Thee, one that shapes toil by command?
They will hunt a righteous person’s soul and condemn innocent blood.

relationship: legal prohibition corresponding to injustice against widows and orphans
rationale: Isaiah condemns seizing the vulnerable people's justice and making widows and orphans prey; Deuteronomy explicitly forbids perverting their judgment and taking a widow's garment as pledge.
source_text: turning aside the judgment of the poor, seizing the justice of My people’s needy, so that a widow becomes their prey and an orphan their plunder.

target_units.text: You shall not pervert the judgment of the sojourner, or of the orphan, or of the widow; neither shall you take a widow’s garment in pledge.
And you shall remember that you were a household slave in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God redeemed you thence; therefore I command you to do this thing.

relationship: parallel inability to escape the approaching judgment day
rationale: Isaiah asks where help or glory can be secured on the day of visitation; Zephaniah describes the approaching day of affliction and denies that silver or gold can rescue anyone. Isaiah's glory is not equated with those metals.
source_text: What will they do on the day of visitation? For affliction will come to you from far away. To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your glory,

target_units.text: For the Lord’s great day is near, near and very swift. The sound of the Lord’s day is bitter and harsh; it is appointed mighty.
That day is a day of wrath, a day of affliction and constraint, a day of untimely ruin and destruction, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist,
a day of trumpet and shouting against fortified cities and high corners.
I will press people hard, and they will walk like the blind because they sinned against the Lord. He will pour out their blood like dust and their flesh like dung.

Their silver and gold will certainly not rescue them on the day of the Lord’s wrath. In the fire of His jealousy all the earth will be consumed, for He will bring completion and haste upon all the earth’s inhabitants.

relationship: repeated literary refrain of continuing anger
rationale: Both units close a description of national punishment with the same refrain: the anger has not turned away and the hand is still high. The preceding punishments differ.
source_text: so as not to fall into captivity? For all these things the anger did not turn away, but the hand is still high.

target_units.text: For Manasseh will eat from Ephraim, and Ephraim from Manasseh, because together they will besiege Judah. For all these things the anger did not turn away, but the hand is still high.

relationship: parallel foreign military power employed in divine judgment
rationale: Isaiah places the rod of divine anger in Assyrian hands; Habakkuk has God raise Chaldean warriors who seize other people's dwellings and captives. The nations are distinct.
source_text: Woe to the Assyrians! The rod of My anger and wrath is in their hands.

target_units.text: For look, I am raising up against you the Chaldean warriors, the bitter and swift nation, who traverse the breadth of the earth to possess dwellings not their own.
Fearsome and conspicuous are they; their judgment will come from themselves, and their claim will proceed from themselves.
Their horses will leap beyond leopards and be fiercer than the wolves of Arabia. Their horsemen will ride out and rush from afar, flying like an eagle eager to eat.
An end will come upon the impious who stand facing them in opposition, and they will gather captives like sand.
They will revel among kings, and tyrants will be their toys; they will mock every fortress, throw up a mound and seize it.

relationship: parallel divine command to attack a city and take spoil
rationale: Isaiah says God will command His people to take spoil and plunder cities; Joshua records God's command to attack Ai and take livestock as spoil. Joshua supplies a different military setting, not an identification of Isaiah's people.
source_text: I will send My anger against a lawless nation, and I will command My people to take spoils and plunder, trample the cities and reduce them to dust.

target_units.text: The Lord said to Joshua, “Do not be afraid or lose heart. Take all the men of war with you, arise, and go up to Ai. Behold, I have delivered the king of Ai and his land into your hands.
Do to Ai as you did to Jericho and its king, and take the livestock as spoil for yourself. Set an ambush behind the city.”

relationship: parallel distinction between divine purpose and a nation's destructive intent
rationale: Isaiah distinguishes the ruler's intention to destroy many nations from the preceding divine commission; Zechariah likewise distinguishes God's limited anger from nations attacking to bring evils.
source_text: But he did not consider it this way and has not reckoned it this way in his soul; rather, his mind will turn aside, even to destroy not a few nations.

target_units.text: and I am angry with great anger at the nations joining in assault, because I was a little angry, but they joined in attacking to bring evils.

relationship: parallel Assyrian boast about conquered countries
rationale: The Assyrian ruler lists earlier conquests, including Samaria; the later Assyrian challenge likewise appeals to the failure of countries' gods to rescue them, explicitly naming Samaria.
source_text: he will say, “Did I not take the country above Babylon and Chalanneh, where the tower was built? I also took Arabia, Damascus and Samaria.

target_units.text: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, saying, “Your God will rescue you.” Have the nations’ gods each rescued his own country from the king of the Assyrians’ hand?
Where is the god of Aimath and Arphath? Where is the god of Seppharim’s city? Were they able to rescue Samaria from my hand?

relationship: parallel imperial claim over dominions and their gods
rationale: Isaiah's ruler claims he will take all dominions and summons Jerusalem's and Samaria's images to wail; the later speech similarly claims no nation's god can rescue its land from Assyrian hands.
source_text: As I took these in my hand, I will also take all the dominions. Wail, carved images in Jerusalem and Samaria!

target_units.text: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, saying, “Your God will rescue you.” Have the nations’ gods each rescued his own country from the king of the Assyrians’ hand?
Where is the god of Aimath and Arphath? Where is the god of Seppharim’s city? Were they able to rescue Samaria from my hand?
Which of all these nations’ gods rescued his land from my hand, that God should rescue Jerusalem from my hand?’”

relationship: close comparison of Samaria's fate with threatened Jerusalem
rationale: Both Assyrian speeches use Samaria's inability to be rescued as the basis for threatening Jerusalem, expressly challenging the protection offered by their gods or images.
source_text: For as I did to Samaria and her handmade objects, so I will also do to Jerusalem and her idols.”

target_units.text: Where is the god of Aimath and Arphath? Where is the god of Seppharim’s city? Were they able to rescue Samaria from my hand?
Which of all these nations’ gods rescued his land from my hand, that God should rescue Jerusalem from my hand?’”

relationship: parallel judgment upon the Assyrian ruler's presumption
rationale: Isaiah promises judgment upon the ruler's great mind and lofty glory; the later oracle rebukes his reproach and raging and promises to turn him back with muzzle and bridle.
source_text: When the Lord has finished doing all things on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, He will bring judgment upon the great mind—the ruler of the Assyrians—and upon the height of the glory of his eyes.

target_units.text: Whom did you reproach and provoke? Against whom did you raise your voice? Yet you did not lift your eyes on high toward the Holy One of Israel.

For through messengers you reproached the Lord. You said, ‘With my many chariots I climbed the mountain heights and the furthest reaches of Lebanon. I cut down its cedar’s height and the cypress’s beauty, and entered the height of a part of the woodland.
I laid a bridge and dried up waters and every gathering of water.’
Did you not hear long ago about these things I did? From ancient days I arranged them; now I have shown them: to desolate nations in strongholds and those dwelling in fortified cities.
I let the hands go, and they withered and became like dry grass on roofs and like wild grass.
But now I know your rest, your going out and your coming in.
Your wrath with which you raged, and your bitterness, have risen to Me. I will put a muzzle in your nose and a bridle in your lips, and turn you back by the way you came.

relationship: parallel Assyrian boasting about personal power in conquest
rationale: Isaiah's ruler boasts that he will remove boundaries and shake cities by strength and understanding; the later speech boasts of chariots and feats of conquest, answered by God's claim to have arranged the devastation.
source_text: For he said, “By strength I will act, and by the wisdom of understanding. I will remove nations’ boundaries, plunder their strength and shake inhabited cities.

target_units.text: For through messengers you reproached the Lord. You said, ‘With my many chariots I climbed the mountain heights and the furthest reaches of Lebanon. I cut down its cedar’s height and the cypress’s beauty, and entered the height of a part of the woodland.
I laid a bridge and dried up waters and every gathering of water.’
Did you not hear long ago about these things I did? From ancient days I arranged them; now I have shown them: to desolate nations in strongholds and those dwelling in fortified cities.

relationship: parallel conqueror's appetite for all nations
rationale: Isaiah's ruler claims the inhabited world as easily seized as abandoned eggs; Habakkuk portrays a boastful man gathering all nations with an appetite like death. Habakkuk's image is not a nest.
source_text: I will seize the whole inhabited world in my hand like a nest, and lift it like abandoned eggs. There is no one who will escape me or contradict me.”

target_units.text: But the wine-soaked, contemptuous, boastful man will accomplish nothing. He widened his appetite like Hades and is like death, never filled; he will gather all nations and receive all peoples to himself.
Will not all these take up a parable against him and a riddle for his account? They will say, ‘Woe to the one multiplying for himself what is not his—how long?—and heavily weighting his collar!’
For suddenly those biting him will rise, and those plotting against you will awake; you will become their plunder.
Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

relationship: related craft analogy rebuking human presumption
rationale: Isaiah denies the tool's glory apart from its wielder; Paul denies the formed object's standing to answer its maker and invokes the potter's authority. The objects and their relationships differ.
source_text: Will an ax be glorified without the one cutting with it, or a saw be raised without the one drawing it? Likewise, if someone lifts a rod or a piece of wood.

target_units.text: But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is formed say to the One who formed it, “Why didst Thou make me this way?”
Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

relationship: parallel fiery wrath joined with dishonor
rationale: Isaiah promises dishonor against honor and fire against glory; the psalm likewise joins pursuing wrath with consuming-fire imagery and a petition that enemies' faces be filled with dishonor.
source_text: And it will not be so; rather, the Lord Sabaoth will send dishonor against your honor, and against your glory a burning fire will burn.

target_units.text: Like fire that will burn through a woodland, as though a flame should burn up mountains,
so Thou wilt pursue them with Thy storm and trouble them in Thy wrath.
Fill their faces with dishonor, and they will seek Thy name, Lord.

relationship: related consuming fire in divine judgment
rationale: Isaiah describes Israel's light becoming fire that consumes woodland like grass; Deuteronomy calls the Lord a consuming fire in its warning against covenant unfaithfulness.
source_text: Israel’s light will become fire, and He will sanctify him in burning fire and consume the woodland like grass. On that day,

target_units.text: For the Lord your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.

relationship: close woodland and mountain fire as judgment imagery
rationale: Isaiah describes mountains, hills and forests consumed in fire; the psalm likewise compares God's pursuit in wrath with fire burning woodland and mountains.
source_text: the mountains, hills and forests will be extinguished, and it will consume from soul to flesh. The one fleeing will be like someone fleeing from a burning flame.

target_units.text: Like fire that will burn through a woodland, as though a flame should burn up mountains,
so Thou wilt pursue them with Thy storm and trouble them in Thy wrath.

relationship: parallel counted remainders after devastation
rationale: Isaiah portrays those left as a number a child will write down; Amos specifies thousands reduced to hundreds and hundreds to tens. Amos supplies numbers but no child recorder.
source_text: Those left from them will be a number, and a child will write them down.

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord: “From the city out of which a thousand went, a hundred will remain, and from the one out of which a hundred went, ten will remain for Israel’s house.”

relationship: close rejection of Assyrian reliance in turning toward God
rationale: Isaiah's survivors will cease trusting their oppressors and trust Israel's Holy One; Hosea commands return to God and declares that Assur will not save them.
source_text: On that day Israel’s remainder will no longer continue, and Jacob’s survivors will certainly no longer trust those who wronged them; rather, they will trust God, Israel’s Holy One, in truth,

target_units.text: Take words with you and return to the Lord your God. Speak to Him so that you do not receive injustice but receive good things, and we will repay the fruit of our lips.
Assur will certainly not save us; we will not mount a horse, and we will certainly no longer call the works of our hands “Our gods.” The One in you will have mercy on an orphan.

relationship: explicit quotation of the saved remnant
rationale: Paul expressly cites Isaiah's contrast between Israel numerous as sea sand and the remnant being saved, continuing with the word completed and cut short.
source_text: Even if Israel’s people becomes like the sea’s sand, their remnant will be saved; for He is completing and cutting short a word in righteousness,

target_units.text: But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel, “Though the number of Israel’s sons be like the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved;
for the Lord will carry out a word on the earth, completing it and cutting it short.”

relationship: explicit quotation of the shortened divine word
rationale: Romans repeats the statement that the Lord carries out a word on earth, completing it and cutting it short; Isaiah specifies the whole inhabited world.
source_text: because God will carry out a shortened word in the whole inhabited world.

target_units.text: for the Lord will carry out a word on the earth, completing it and cutting it short.”

relationship: close reassurance against fear of Assyria
rationale: The Lord tells Zion not to fear the Assyrians; the later message through Isaiah likewise tells Hezekiah not to fear their envoys' words and announces the ruler's return and death.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord Sabaoth: “Do not fear the Assyrians, My people dwelling in Zion, because he will strike you with a rod; for I bring a blow upon you to see Egypt’s way.

target_units.text: and Isaiah said to them, “You shall say this to your master: Thus says the Lord: Do not fear the words you heard, with which the king of the Assyrians’ envoys reproached Me.
Behold, I will put a spirit into him. On hearing a report he will return to his country, and he will fall by the sword in his own land.”

relationship: parallel short duration of divine anger
rationale: Isaiah says wrath will cease after a little while; the later promise likewise contrasts a short abandonment and little anger with great, everlasting mercy. The anger against hostile counsel is additional here.
source_text: For yet a little while, and the wrath will cease, but My anger will be against their counsel.”

target_units.text: “For a short time I abandoned you, and with great mercy I will have mercy on you.
In a little anger I turned My face from you, and with everlasting mercy I will have mercy on you,” says the Lord who rescued you.

relationship: explicit historical comparison with God's blow against Midian
rationale: Isaiah recalls Midian's defeat as a pattern of divine action; Judges describes the Lord turning the camp's swords against itself and Israel capturing Midian's rulers.
source_text: God will rouse action against them according to Midian’s blow in a place of affliction, and His anger on the way by the sea, toward the way by Egypt.

target_units.text: The three hundred horn trumpets sounded, and the Lord set each man’s sword against his neighbour throughout the camp. The camp fled as far as Beth-shittah and, gathered together, as far as the edge of Abel-meholah and toward Tabbath.
The men of Israel cried out from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh, and they pursued Midian.

Gideon sent messengers throughout Ephraim’s territory, saying, “Go down to meet Midian and seize for yourselves the water as far as Beth-barah, and the Jordan.” All the men of Ephraim cried out, and they seized the water beforehand as far as Beth-barah, and the Jordan.
They captured Midian’s two rulers, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb in Sourin and Zeeb in Jakephzeeb, and pursued Midian. They brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon from beyond the Jordan.

relationship: historical counterpart of divine action by the Egyptian sea
rationale: Isaiah also invokes God's anger on the way by the sea toward Egypt; Exodus records the Egyptians overwhelmed in the sea and Israel rescued by the Lord's great hand.
source_text: God will rouse action against them according to Midian’s blow in a place of affliction, and His anger on the way by the sea, toward the way by Egypt.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and toward daybreak the water returned to its place. The Egyptians fled beneath the water, and the Lord shook the Egyptians into the midst of the sea.
The water returned and covered the chariots, the riders, and all Pharaoh’s force that had entered the sea after them. Not one of them remained.
But the sons of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.
The Lord rescued Israel that day from the Egyptians’ hand, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
Israel saw the great hand in what the Lord had done to the Egyptians. The people feared the Lord and trusted God and His attendant Moses.

relationship: close destruction of an oppressive yoke
rationale: Isaiah promises removal and destruction of the yoke from the shoulders; Jeremiah likewise promises God will smash the yoke from the neck and end service to foreigners.
source_text: On that day his fear will be removed from you and his yoke from your shoulder, and the yoke will be destroyed from your shoulders.

target_units.text: On that day, said the Lord, I will smash the yoke from their neck and tear apart their bonds, and they will no longer work for foreigners.

relationship: parallel downfall of exalted power in a tree portrayal
rationale: Isaiah promises the shattering of the insolently lofty before Lebanon's fall; Ezekiel's Assyrian tree, used in an address to Pharaoh, is handed over for destruction after rising high.
source_text: For behold, the Master, the Lord Sabaoth, throws the glorious ones into confusion with strength; those lofty in insolence will be shattered, and the high brought low,

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord: Because you became great in size and set your crown amid clouds, and I saw it being lifted high,
I handed it into the hands of a ruler of nations, and he brought about its destruction.

Foreigners, scourges from nations, utterly destroyed it and cast it upon the mountains. Its branches fell in all the ravines; its trunks were shattered in every plain of the land. All the nations’ peoples went down from their shelter and dashed it to the ground.
All the sky’s birds rested upon its fallen trunk, and all the field’s beasts were upon its trunks,

so that none of the trees in the water may rise high in their size. They did not set their crowns amid clouds, and none of those drinking water stood toward them in their height. All were given to death, to the depth of the earth, among human beings, with those descending to a pit.

relationship: close Lebanon imagery joined with downfall and the sword
rationale: Isaiah joins Lebanon's fall with the high falling by a sword; Ezekiel likewise describes Lebanon's trees descending with those wounded by the sword in its account of imperial downfall.
source_text: and the high will fall by a sword, while Lebanon will fall with the high.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord, the Lord: On the day it descended to Hades, the abyss mourned it. I stopped its rivers and restrained the multitude of water. Lebanon grew dark over it, and all the plain’s trees collapsed over it.

At the sound of its fall the nations shook when I brought it down to Hades with those descending to a pit. In the earth all the trees of delight and the choice trees of Lebanon, all drinking water, comforted it.
For they too went down with it to Hades among those wounded by the sword; its offspring, those living under its shelter, perished in the midst of their life.

Whom were you likened to? Descend and be brought down with the trees of delight into the earth’s depth. Among the uncircumcised you will lie with those wounded by the sword. So it is with Pharaoh and the multitude of his strength, says the Lord, the Lord.’”

relationship: related descent from Jesse through David
rationale: Isaiah announces a shoot from Jesse's root; Acts explicitly identifies David as Jesse's son and Jesus as the Savior brought from David's seed according to promise.
source_text: And a shoot will come from the root of Jesse, and a blossom will rise from the root.

target_units.text: After removing him, He raised up David as king for them, to whom He also bore witness, saying, ‘I have found David son of Jesse, a man after My heart, who will do all My will.’
From this man’s seed, according to promise, God brought Israel a Savior, Jesus,

relationship: close Spirit resting and remaining upon the promised figure
rationale: Isaiah says God's Spirit will rest upon the shoot from Jesse; John testifies that the Spirit descended and remained upon Jesus. Isaiah additionally enumerates the Spirit's qualities.
source_text: And the Spirit of God will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness.

target_units.text: And John testified, saying, “I have beheld the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and He remained upon Him.
And I did not know Him, but the One who sent me to baptize in water said to me, ‘The One upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining—this is the One who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’
And I have seen and have testified that this is the Son of God.”

relationship: close rejection of judgment by appearance
rationale: Isaiah's figure will not judge according to appearance; Jesus likewise commands judgment according to righteousness rather than appearance.
source_text: The spirit of the fear of God will fill him. He will not judge according to appearance, nor reprove according to report;

target_units.text: Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment.”

relationship: close royal judgment for poor and lowly people
rationale: Isaiah describes judging the cause of the lowly; the royal psalm likewise asks that the king judge the poor in justice and save the needy person's children.
source_text: but he will judge the cause of the lowly, and reprove the lowly of the earth; and he will strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and with breath through his lips he will slay the ungodly.

target_units.text: to judge Thy people in righteousness, and Thy poor in justice.
Let the mountains take up peace for Thy people, and the hills in righteousness.
He will judge the poor of the people, and save the children of the needy, and humble the false accuser,

relationship: close slaying of the lawless by breath from the mouth
rationale: Isaiah says the figure will slay the ungodly with breath through his lips; Paul describes the Lord Jesus killing the lawless one with the breath of His mouth.
source_text: but he will judge the cause of the lowly, and reprove the lowly of the earth; and he will strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and with breath through his lips he will slay the ungodly.

target_units.text: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of His mouth and bring to nothing by the manifestation of His coming.

relationship: close righteousness and truth portrayed as bodily equipment
rationale: Isaiah binds righteousness and truth around the figure's loins and sides; Paul fastens truth around the believers' waist and adds a breastplate of righteousness. Their arrangement differs.
source_text: His loins will be girded with righteousness, and his sides bound with truth.

target_units.text: Stand, therefore, having fastened truth around your waist and put on the breastplate of righteousness,

relationship: close wolf and lamb feeding together
rationale: Both portray wolves and lambs feeding together in the restored order. The later verse does not repeat this verse's leopard, young goat or child leading the animals.
source_text: And the wolf will feed with the lamb, and the leopard will rest with the young goat; and the calf and the bull and the lion will feed together, and a little child will lead them.

target_units.text: Then wolves and lambs will graze together, and a lion will eat straw like an ox, while a serpent will eat earth like bread. They will not wrong or destroy on My holy mountain,” says the Lord.

relationship: close lion eating straw like an ox
rationale: Both portray the lion eating straw together with, or like, the ox. The later verse does not repeat the bear and shared young described here.
source_text: And the ox and the bear will feed together, and their young will be together; and the lion and the ox will eat straw together.

target_units.text: Then wolves and lambs will graze together, and a lion will eat straw like an ox, while a serpent will eat earth like bread. They will not wrong or destroy on My holy mountain,” says the Lord.

relationship: related protection from dangerous serpents
rationale: Isaiah pictures an infant reaching over asps' holes, within 11:9's promise of no harm; Jesus promises His messengers authority over snakes and protection from harm. The people and actions differ.
source_text: And an infant will stretch out his hand over the hole of asps, and over the nest of their young.

target_units.text: Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions, and over all the enemy’s power, and nothing will ever harm you.

relationship: close earth filled with divine knowledge compared with covering water
rationale: Both announce the earth filled with knowledge of the Lord or His glory and compare this with covering water. Isaiah specifically names the seas.
source_text: And they will certainly do no harm, nor will they be able at all to destroy anyone upon My holy mountain; for the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas.

target_units.text: For the earth will be filled with knowing the Lord’s glory, as water will cover them.

relationship: close absence of harm upon God's holy mountain
rationale: Both expressly deny harm or destruction upon God's holy mountain, alongside the portrayal of formerly dangerous animals living peacefully.
source_text: And they will certainly do no harm, nor will they be able at all to destroy anyone upon My holy mountain; for the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas.

target_units.text: Then wolves and lambs will graze together, and a lion will eat straw like an ox, while a serpent will eat earth like bread. They will not wrong or destroy on My holy mountain,” says the Lord.

relationship: explicit quotation of Jesse's root and the nations' hope
rationale: Paul expressly quotes Isaiah's root of Jesse rising to rule nations and becoming the object of their hope. Isaiah additionally describes his rest as honor.
source_text: On that day there will be Jesse’s root and the one rising to rule nations; nations will hope in him, and his rest will be honor.

target_units.text: And again Isaiah says, “There will be the root of Jesse, and the One who rises to rule Gentiles; upon Him Gentiles will hope.”

relationship: parallel renewed divine care for a people dispersed among nations
rationale: Isaiah enumerates nations from which the remaining people come under God's renewed action, leading into 11:12's gathering; Deuteronomy promises renewed mercy and gathering from the nations of dispersion.
source_text: On that day the Lord will again show His hand, to be zealous for the remaining remnant of the people left from the Assyrians, Egypt, Babylonia, Ethiopia, the Elamites, the sun’s rising and Arabia.

target_units.text: then the Lord shall heal your sins, and have mercy upon you, and shall gather you again from all the nations whither the Lord has scattered you.
If your dispersion is from one end of heaven unto the other end of heaven, from thence shall the Lord your God gather you, and from thence shall the Lord your God take you.
And the Lord your God shall bring you into the land which your fathers inherited, and you shall inherit it; and He shall do you good, and make you more numerous than your fathers.

relationship: shared gathering from the four quarters and furthest reaches
rationale: Isaiah gathers Israel and Judah from the earth's four wings; Matthew describes angels gathering the chosen from four winds and the heavens' extremities. Matthew does not name Israel and Judah here.
source_text: He will raise a signal to the nations and gather Israel’s lost ones; He will gather Judah’s scattered ones from the earth’s four wings.

target_units.text: He will send His angels with a great trumpet, and they will gather His chosen from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other.

relationship: close reconciliation of Ephraim and Judah
rationale: Isaiah ends Ephraim's jealousy and Judah's affliction of Ephraim; Ezekiel joins Ephraim and Judah in one staff and promises they will no longer be two kingdoms.
source_text: Ephraim’s jealousy will be removed, and Judah’s enemies will perish. Ephraim will not envy Judah, and Judah will not afflict Ephraim.

target_units.text: say to them, Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will take Joseph’s tribe through Ephraim’s hand, and Israel’s tribes attached to him, and place them upon Judah’s tribe. They will become one staff in Judah’s hand.
The staffs upon which you wrote will be in your hand before them,

and say to them, Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am taking all Israel’s house from among the nations where they entered, gathering them from all those around them and bringing them into Israel’s land.
I will make them one nation in My land and upon Israel’s mountains, and one ruler will be theirs. They will no longer be two nations or ever again be divided into two kingdoms,

relationship: parallel united Israelite victory over Edom
rationale: After Judah and Ephraim's reconciliation, Isaiah depicts joint victory including Idumea; Obadiah likewise joins Jacob's and Joseph's houses against Esau and his mountain. The wider lists of territories differ.
source_text: They will fly in foreigners’ ships toward the sea; together they will plunder those from the sun’s rising and Idumea. Upon Moab they will first lay their hands, and Ammon’s sons will be the first to obey.

target_units.text: The house of Jacob will be a fire, the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble. They will blaze against them and consume them, and there will be no bearer of fire in the house of Esau, because the Lord has spoken.

Those in the Negeb will possess the mountain of Esau, and those in the Shephelah will possess the foreigners. They will possess the mountain of Ephraim, the plain of Samaria, Benjamin and the land of Gilead.

And this is the beginning of the deportation: for the sons of Israel, the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath; and the deportation of Jerusalem as far as Ephrathah. They will inherit the cities of the Negeb.
And men who have been saved shall ascend from Mount Zion to execute judgment upon the mountain of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the Lord’s.

relationship: close wind-driven opening of a passage across waters
rationale: Isaiah describes God's hand and violent wind opening passage through waters; Exodus records Moses stretching his hand and the Lord's violent south wind making the sea dry. Isaiah additionally names seven ravines.
source_text: The Lord will lay Egypt’s sea waste and bring His hand upon the river with a violent wind. He will strike seven ravines so that one may pass through it in sandals.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The Lord drove the sea back with a violent south wind all night and made the sea dry. The water was split.
The sons of Israel entered the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.

relationship: explicit historical comparison with Israel's departure from Egypt
rationale: Isaiah names the day Israel left Egypt as the pattern for the remnant's passage; Exodus records Israel's dry crossing and rescue from the Egyptians.
source_text: There will be a passage for My remaining people in Egypt, and it will be for Israel as on the day it came out of Egypt’s land.

target_units.text: But the sons of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.
The Lord rescued Israel that day from the Egyptians’ hand, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
Israel saw the great hand in what the Lord had done to the Egyptians. The people feared the Lord and trusted God and His attendant Moses.

relationship: close thanksgiving for divine wrath turned away
rationale: Isaiah thanks God because anger was turned away and mercy given; the psalm likewise recalls forgiven sins, stopped wrath and anger turned away.
source_text: On that day you will say, “I will bless Thee, Lord, because Thou wast angry with me, didst turn Thy wrath away and have mercy on me.

target_units.text: Thou forgavest Thy people their acts of lawlessness; Thou didst cover all their sins. Diapsalma.
Thou didst stop all Thy wrath; Thou didst turn away from the anger of Thy fury.

relationship: close confession that the Lord has become salvation
rationale: Isaiah calls the Lord his glory and praise and says He became his salvation; the psalm likewise calls Him strength and hymn and says He has become salvation.
source_text: Behold, my God, my Savior, is the Lord; I will trust in Him and be saved in Him, and I will not fear, because the Lord is my glory and my praise, and He became my salvation.”

target_units.text: The Lord is my strength and my hymn, and He has become my salvation.

relationship: close freedom from fear through the Lord's saving protection
rationale: Isaiah trusts the saving Lord and refuses fear; the psalm likewise calls Him Savior and protector, asks whom to fear, and maintains hope even amid war.
source_text: Behold, my God, my Savior, is the Lord; I will trust in Him and be saved in Him, and I will not fear, because the Lord is my glory and my praise, and He became my salvation.”

target_units.text: Of David, before being anointed. The Lord is my light and my Savior; whom will I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom will I be afraid?
When those doing evil approached me to eat my flesh, those who afflict me and my enemies, they grew weak and fell.
Even if an army draws up against me, my heart will not fear; even if war rises against me, in this I hope.

relationship: related saving water described as a spring
rationale: Isaiah promises joyful drawing from salvation's springs; Jesus promises water becoming a spring into eternal life within its recipient. The setting and manner of receiving the water differ.
source_text: You will draw water with gladness from salvation’s springs.

target_units.text: Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God and who it is who says to you, ‘Give Me a drink,’ you would have asked Him, and He would have given you living water.”
The woman said to Him, “Sir, Thou hast no vessel for drawing water, and the well is deep. Where, then, dost Thou get this living water?
Art Thou greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, and his sons and his livestock?”
Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again.
But whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will certainly never thirst; rather, the water I will give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life.”

relationship: close summons to call God's name and proclaim His works among nations
rationale: Both direct the hearers to invoke the Lord's name and announce His works among the nations, joining that announcement with song and praise of His name.
source_text: On that day you will say, “Sing hymns to the Lord, cry out His name, announce His glorious deeds among the nations, remember that His name was exalted.

target_units.text: Hallelujah. Give thanks to the Lord and call upon His name; announce His works among the nations.
Sing to Him and make music to Him; recount all His wonders.
Be praised in His holy name; let the heart of those seeking the Lord rejoice.

relationship: parallel song for divine wonders made known throughout the earth
rationale: Isaiah commands song because of God's exalted deeds and their worldwide announcement; the psalm likewise calls for song for His wonders and declares salvation known to the earth's ends.
source_text: Sing the Lord’s name, because He has done exalted things; announce these throughout the earth.

target_units.text: A psalm of David. Sing to the Lord a new song, for the Lord has done wonders. His right hand and His holy arm won salvation for Him.
The Lord made His salvation known; before the nations He revealed His righteousness.
He remembered His mercy to Jacob and His truth to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God.

relationship: close Zion rejoicing because God is within her
rationale: Both summon Zion or Jerusalem to gladness and ground that joy in the presence of Israel's God within her.
source_text: Exult and be glad, you who dwell in Zion, because Israel’s Holy One has been exalted in her midst.”

target_units.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion! Proclaim, daughter Jerusalem! Be glad and delight with all your heart, daughter Jerusalem!
The Lord removed your wrongdoings and has redeemed you from your enemies’ hand. The Lord, King of Israel, is within you; you will see evils no more.
At that time the Lord will say to Jerusalem, “Take courage, Zion; do not let your hands hang loose.
The Lord your God is within you; mighty, He shall save you. He shall bring gladness upon you, and renew you in His love; and He shall rejoice over you with delight, as on a day of feasting.”

relationship: parallel prophetic oracle against Babylon
rationale: Both introduce a divine oracle against Babylon and proceed to describe her capture and devastation. Isaiah names his vision; Jeremiah introduces the Lord's spoken word.
source_text: The vision that Isaiah son of Amos saw against Babylon.

target_units.text: The Lord’s word that He spoke against Babylon:
Announce among the nations and make it heard; do not hide it. Say, Babylon has been captured! Bel was disgraced, the fearless one; the delicate one was handed over, Marodach.
A nation came up against her from the north; it will make her land a ruin, with no one living in it, from human to livestock.

relationship: close military summons to raise a signal
rationale: Isaiah's Babylon vision commands a signal on a level mountain; Jeremiah's Babylon oracle commands a signal on her walls alongside guards and weapons. The specified sites differ.
source_text: Raise a signal on a level mountain, lift your voice to them, do not fear, beckon with the hand: “Open, rulers!”

target_units.text: Raise a signal on Babylon’s walls; set up quivers, raise guards, prepare weapons, for the Lord has undertaken and will do what He spoke against Babylon’s inhabitants,

relationship: close consecration of forces for judgment against Babylon
rationale: Isaiah describes God commanding and leading consecrated forces to fulfill His wrath; Jeremiah likewise commands consecrating nations against Babylon. Jeremiah names the Medes rather than Isaiah's giants.
source_text: I command, and I lead them; they are consecrated, and I lead them. Giants are coming to fulfill My wrath, rejoicing and acting insolently together.

target_units.text: Raise a signal on the earth; sound a trumpet among the nations. Consecrate nations against her; give orders against her to Ararat’s kingdoms from Me and to the Ashkenazites. Set up arrow batteries against her; bring up horses against her like a multitude of locusts.
Consecrate nations against her: the king of the Medes and of all the earth, his leaders and all his generals.

relationship: close gathering of nations for the assault on Babylon
rationale: Isaiah describes sounds of kings and gathered nations and names the Lord's command to an armed nation; Jeremiah likewise has God rouse assemblies of nations to deploy against Babylon and capture her.
source_text: A sound of many nations upon the mountains, like many nations; a sound of kings and gathered nations. The Lord Sabaoth has commanded an armed nation,

target_units.text: I am rousing assemblies of nations against Babylon from the north. They will deploy against her; from there she will be captured. Like a discerning warrior’s missile, it will not return empty.

relationship: close armed force arriving from afar
rationale: Both describe an armed force from a distant extremity within an oracle against Babylon. Isaiah extends the devastation to the inhabited world; Jeremiah explicitly directs the force against daughter Babylon.
source_text: to come from a distant land, from the farthest edge of heaven’s foundation—the Lord and His armed fighters—to destroy the whole inhabited world.

target_units.text: A people is coming from the north; a great nation and many kings will be roused from the earth’s farthest part,
holding bow and dagger. It is insolent and certainly will not show mercy. Their voice will sound like the sea. They will ride horses, prepared like fire for war against you, daughter Babylon.

relationship: close lament over the approaching day of the Lord
rationale: Both call for lament because the Lord's day is near. Isaiah describes shattering from God; Joel describes the day coming like suffering.
source_text: Wail, for the Lord’s day is near, and shattering will come from God.

target_units.text: “Alas, alas, alas for the day! For the Lord’s day is near, and it will come like suffering from suffering.”

relationship: close disabled hands in terror of Babylon's fall
rationale: Isaiah says every hand will slacken and every soul grow cowardly; Jeremiah likewise describes Babylon's king hearing the invaders' report and his hands becoming disabled.
source_text: Therefore every hand will slacken, and every human soul grow cowardly;

target_units.text: Babylon’s king heard the report about them, and his hands were disabled. Distress seized him, birth pains like a woman giving birth.

relationship: close birth-pain image for terror at Babylon's fall
rationale: Isaiah's troubled envoys are seized by labor pains like a woman giving birth; Jeremiah applies that same comparison to Babylon's distressed king. Isaiah additionally describes faces changing as to flame.
source_text: the envoys will be troubled, and labor pains will hold them like those of a woman giving birth. They will lament to one another and be distraught, and change their face as to flame.

target_units.text: Babylon’s king heard the report about them, and his hands were disabled. Distress seized him, birth pains like a woman giving birth.

relationship: close day of wrath bringing destruction upon sinners
rationale: Both describe the Lord's day as wrath and destruction, link the judgment with human sin, and extend its destructive scope across the earth.
source_text: For behold, the Lord’s incurable day comes, of wrath and anger, to make the whole inhabited world deserted and destroy its sinners from it.

target_units.text: That day is a day of wrath, a day of affliction and constraint, a day of untimely ruin and destruction, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist,
a day of trumpet and shouting against fortified cities and high corners.
I will press people hard, and they will walk like the blind because they sinned against the Lord. He will pour out their blood like dust and their flesh like dung.

Their silver and gold will certainly not rescue them on the day of the Lord’s wrath. In the fire of His jealousy all the earth will be consumed, for He will bring completion and haste upon all the earth’s inhabitants.

relationship: close prophetic darkening of sun and moon
rationale: Both portray the sun and moon losing light alongside a disruption of the stars. Isaiah's stars cease shining, including Orion; Matthew's stars fall from heaven.
source_text: For heaven’s stars, Orion and all heaven’s array will not give light; it will grow dark as the sun rises, and the moon will not give its light.

target_units.text: Immediately after the affliction of those days, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its brightness, the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

relationship: parallel divine judgment lowering insolence
rationale: Isaiah promises the destruction of lawless insolence and lowering of the proud; Jeremiah likewise addresses insolent Babylon and declares that her insolence will weaken and fall.
source_text: I will ordain evils for the whole inhabited world, and for the ungodly their sins; I will destroy the insolence of the lawless and lower the insolence of the proud.

target_units.text: I am against you, insolent woman, says the Lord, for your day has come, the time of your vengeance.
Your insolence will grow weak and fall, with no one to raise it. I will kindle fire in her forest, and it will devour everything around her.

relationship: shared comparison of human worth with gold
rationale: Isaiah calls the remaining person more precious than gold; Lamentations calls Zion's sons precious and exalted in gold while lamenting their treatment as earthen vessels. The valuations move in different directions.
source_text: Those left will be more precious than unrefined gold, and a human being more precious than the stone from Souphir.

target_units.text: Zion’s precious sons, exalted in gold— how they were regarded as earthen vessels, works of a potter’s hands!

relationship: close earth shaking under divine judgment
rationale: Isaiah joins the earth's shaking from its foundations with the Lord's fury; Jeremiah likewise says the earth shook when the Lord's purpose rose against Babylon.
source_text: For heaven will be enraged, and the earth shaken from its foundations through the fury of the Lord Sabaoth’s anger, on the day when His wrath comes upon it.

target_units.text: The earth was shaken and suffered, for the Lord’s purpose rose against Babylon, to make Babylon’s land a ruin, no longer inhabited.

relationship: close flight to one's own people and country from Babylon
rationale: Both describe people turning or fleeing to their own people and land during Babylon's devastation. Isaiah adds fleeing-gazelle and wandering-sheep images; Jeremiah names the Greek sword.
source_text: Those left will be like a fleeing little gazelle and a wandering sheep, with no one to gather them, so that each turns back to his own people and hastens to his own country.

target_units.text: Destroy seed from Babylon, the one holding a sickle at harvest. Before the Greek sword, each will return to his people and flee to his land.

relationship: parallel fallen people in the assault on Babylon
rationale: Isaiah announces defeat of those captured and death by sword for those gathered; Jeremiah likewise describes wounded and pierced people falling in the Chaldeans' land during the assault.
source_text: Whoever is captured will be defeated, and those gathered together will fall by a sword.

target_units.text: Against her let the archer stretch his bow, and let the man who has armor put it on. Do not spare her young men; obliterate her whole force.
Wounded men will fall in the Chaldeans’ land, and pierced men outside her.

relationship: close dashing of Babylon's children in retribution
rationale: Isaiah predicts children dashed before their parents in Babylon's judgment; the psalm addresses daughter Babylon and pronounces happy the one dashing her infants against a rock. Their speech forms differ.
source_text: They will dash their children before them, plunder their houses and take possession of their wives.

target_units.text: Daughter Babylon, miserable one, happy is the one who will repay you the repayment you gave us.
Happy is the one who will seize your infants and dash them against the rock.

relationship: parallel seizure of homes and wives in national judgment
rationale: Isaiah also announces houses plundered and wives taken; Jeremiah likewise describes houses, fields and wives transferred to others. Jeremiah's surrounding warning concerns Jerusalem rather than Babylon.
source_text: They will dash their children before them, plunder their houses and take possession of their wives.

target_units.text: And I filled up My fury and held back and did not bring them to an end. I will pour it upon little children outside and upon a gathering of young men together, because man and woman will be seized, the elder with one full of days.
And their houses will be transferred to others, fields and their wives together, because I will stretch out My hand against those dwelling in this land, says the Lord.

relationship: close divine rousing of the Medes against Babylon
rationale: Isaiah expressly announces God rousing the Medes; Jeremiah likewise says the Lord roused the Medes' king to destroy Babylon. Isaiah additionally denies their interest in silver or gold.
source_text: Behold, I am rousing the Medes against you, who do not value silver or have need of gold.

target_units.text: Prepare the arrows; fill the quivers. The Lord roused the spirit of the Medes’ king, for His anger against Babylon is to destroy her. This is the Lord’s vengeance, vengeance for His people.

relationship: close invading force without mercy for the young
rationale: Isaiah denies the invading force's pity for children; Deuteronomy likewise warns of a distant invading nation without mercy for the young. Deuteronomy addresses Israel, while Isaiah's oracle concerns Babylon.
source_text: They will shatter young men’s arrows and certainly not pity your children; their eyes will not spare the children.

target_units.text: The Lord shall bring against you a nation from afar, from the end of the earth, as the swooping of an eagle, a nation whose speech you shall not understand,
a nation shameless of countenance, which shall not regard the face of the aged, nor have mercy upon the young.

relationship: explicit historical comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah
rationale: Isaiah names God's overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah as Babylon's pattern; Genesis records the fire and sulfur and the overthrow of those cities and their surrounding country.
source_text: Babylon, which is called glorious by the king of the Chaldeans, will be as when God overturned Sodom and Gomorrah.

target_units.text: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of the heaven;
and He overthrew those cities, and all the surrounding country, and all that lived in the cities, and all that sprang from the earth.

relationship: close parallel application of Sodom's overthrow to Babylon
rationale: Both Babylon oracles explicitly compare her devastation with God's overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah. Jeremiah further draws out the absence of human residents.
source_text: Babylon, which is called glorious by the king of the Chaldeans, will be as when God overturned Sodom and Gomorrah.

target_units.text: As God overturned Sodom, Gomorrah, and their bordering places, said the Lord, no person will live there, and no human being will reside there.

relationship: close promise that Babylon will remain uninhabited
rationale: Both deny future habitation in Babylon. Isaiah specifically excludes Arabs passing through and shepherds resting there; Jeremiah speaks generally of no human residing there.
source_text: She will not be inhabited for everlasting time, nor will people ever enter her through many generations. Arabs will certainly not pass through her, and shepherds will certainly not rest in her.

target_units.text: Therefore apparitions will live on the islands, and daughters of sirens will live in her. She certainly will never again be inhabited.
As God overturned Sodom, Gomorrah, and their bordering places, said the Lord, no person will live there, and no human being will reside there.

relationship: close uncanny inhabitants of abandoned Babylon
rationale: Isaiah fills the deserted place with wild beasts, sirens and dancing demons; Jeremiah likewise mentions apparitions on the islands and daughters of sirens living in her, while denying human habitation. The inhabitants differ in detail.
source_text: Wild beasts will rest there, and the houses fill with sound; sirens will rest there, and demons dance there.

target_units.text: Therefore apparitions will live on the islands, and daughters of sirens will live in her. She certainly will never again be inhabited.

relationship: close ruined territory occupied by donkey-centaurs and nesting hedgehogs
rationale: Both name donkey-centaurs dwelling in a devastated place and hedgehogs nesting there. Isaiah 34's oracle concerns Idumea, while this oracle concerns Babylon.
source_text: Donkey-centaurs will dwell there, and hedgehogs make nests in their houses. It comes quickly and will not delay.

target_units.text: Birds, hedgehogs, ibises and ravens will dwell in her; a measuring cord for deserted land will be cast upon her, and donkey-centaurs will dwell in her.
Her rulers will be no more, for her kings, her rulers and her magnates will come to destruction.
Thorny trees will sprout in their cities and her fortifications; she will become a dwelling for sirens and a courtyard for ostriches.
Demons will meet donkey-centaurs and cry one to another. There donkey-centaurs will rest, for they found rest for themselves.
There a hedgehog nested, and the earth kept her children safe. There deer met and saw one another’s faces;

relationship: related assurance that an announced coming will not linger
rationale: Isaiah closes Babylon's desolation with an assurance of speedy arrival without delay; Habakkuk likewise assures that the awaited one will come and not linger. The announced subjects differ.
source_text: Donkey-centaurs will dwell there, and hedgehogs make nests in their houses. It comes quickly and will not delay.

target_units.text: For the vision is still for a season, and it will rise toward the end and not toward emptiness. If he delays, wait for him, for coming he will come and certainly will not linger.

relationship: close renewed mercy and choice of God's people or city
rationale: Isaiah promises renewed pity and choice of Jacob and Israel; Zechariah likewise promises renewed mercy upon Zion and renewed choice of Jerusalem.
source_text: The Lord will pity Jacob and again choose Israel; they will rest upon their land, and the resident foreigner will be added to them and added to Jacob’s house,

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem in compassion, and My house will be rebuilt in her, says the Lord Almighty, and a measure will again be extended over Jerusalem.”
The angel speaking within me said to me, “Cry out: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Cities will again overflow with good things; the Lord will again have mercy on Zion and again choose Jerusalem.”

relationship: close inclusion of resident foreigners in Israel's restored land
rationale: Isaiah adds the resident foreigner to Jacob's house as Israel rests upon its land; Ezekiel likewise gives sojourners a share in the tribal inheritance alongside native Israelites.
source_text: The Lord will pity Jacob and again choose Israel; they will rest upon their land, and the resident foreigner will be added to them and added to Jacob’s house,

target_units.text: You will cast lots for it for yourselves and for the sojourners dwelling among you who have fathered sons among you. They will be to you as native-born among the sons of Israel; with you they will eat from an inheritance among Israel’s tribes.
They will be in a tribe of sojourners, among the sojourners who are with them; there you will give them an inheritance, says the Lord God.

relationship: close reversal of possession and captivity
rationale: Isaiah promises that former captors will become captives and rulers be ruled; Obadiah similarly says Jacob's house will possess those who possessed them.
source_text: and nations will take them and bring them into their place; they will inherit and multiply upon God’s land as male and female slaves. Those who took them captive will be captives, and those who ruled them will be ruled.

target_units.text: But on Mount Zion there will be salvation, and it will be holy; the house of Jacob will possess those who possessed them.

relationship: parallel divine release from oppressive slavery
rationale: Isaiah promises rest from harsh slavery and pain; Exodus likewise has God hear Israel's enslaved groaning and promise rescue from Egyptian domination and oppression.
source_text: On that day God will give you rest from pain, your wrath and the harsh slavery in which you served them,

target_units.text: I have heard the groaning of the sons of Israel, whom the Egyptians enslave, and I have remembered your covenant.
Go, say to the sons of Israel: ‘I am the Lord. I will bring you out from the Egyptians’ domination and deliver you from slavery. I will ransom you with an uplifted arm and with great judgment.
And I will take you to Myself for a people, and I will be your God; and you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from the oppression of the Egyptians.

relationship: parallel lament or taunt directed against a conqueror
rationale: Isaiah introduces a lament over Babylon's king and the taskmaster's rest; Habakkuk introduces a parable and riddle against the man gathering nations, announcing that the plunderer will be plundered.
source_text: and you will take up this lament against Babylon’s king and say on that day, “How the one who made demands has rested, and the taskmaster rested!

target_units.text: But the wine-soaked, contemptuous, boastful man will accomplish nothing. He widened his appetite like Hades and is like death, never filled; he will gather all nations and receive all peoples to himself.
Will not all these take up a parable against him and a riddle for his account? They will say, ‘Woe to the one multiplying for himself what is not his—how long?—and heavily weighting his collar!’
For suddenly those biting him will rise, and those plotting against you will awake; you will become their plunder.
Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

relationship: close divine shattering of an oppressive yoke
rationale: Isaiah says God shattered sinners' and rulers' yokes; Jeremiah likewise promises that God will smash the yoke and end service to foreigners.
source_text: God shattered the sinners’ yoke, the rulers’ yoke;

target_units.text: On that day, said the Lord, I will smash the yoke from their neck and tear apart their bonds, and they will no longer work for foreigners.

relationship: parallel rejoicing at an oppressor's downfall
rationale: Isaiah describes the whole earth crying with gladness as the taskmaster rests; Nahum describes those hearing the report clapping over the one whose evil had continually reached them.
source_text: he rested confidently. The whole earth cries out with gladness,

target_units.text: There is no healing for your crushing; your wound has become inflamed. All who hear the report of you will clap their hands over you, for upon whom has your evil not continually come?

relationship: shared personification of trees rejoicing at judgment
rationale: Isaiah's Lebanon trees rejoice because the cutter no longer comes after the king's fall; the psalm likewise portrays woodland trees exulting before the Lord as He comes to judge.
source_text: and Lebanon’s trees rejoiced over you, and Lebanon’s cedar: ‘Since you have fallen asleep, the one cutting us has not come up.’

target_units.text: The plains will rejoice, and everything in them; then all the trees of the woodland will exult
before the Lord, for He is coming, for He is coming to judge the earth. He will judge the inhabited world with righteousness and peoples with His truth.

relationship: close underworld scene with giants addressing a fallen power
rationale: Isaiah depicts Hades receiving the fallen ruler among giants and kings; Ezekiel likewise gives giants speech from the pit and places Assyria's assembly among the dead there.
source_text: Hades below grew bitter on meeting you. All the giants who ruled the earth rose together for you, those who raised all the nations’ kings from their thrones.

target_units.text: The giants will say to you, ‘Be in the depth of a pit! Whom do you surpass? Descend and lie with the uncircumcised among those wounded by the sword.’
