There Assyria and all his assembly, all wounded, were placed. Their burial is in the depth of a pit, and his assembly was around his tomb, all the wounded who fell by the sword,

relationship: close inclusion of a ruler among previously fallen powers
rationale: Isaiah's dead rulers number Babylon's ruler among themselves; Ezekiel likewise says Pharaoh too will lie among the wounded and describes rulers already there. In Ezekiel the prediction is spoken by God.
source_text: They will all answer and say to you, ‘You too were captured as we were, and were numbered among us.’

target_units.text: You too will lie among the uncircumcised with those wounded by the sword.
There were placed Assyria’s rulers, who gave his strength to a sword wound. These lay with the wounded, with those descending to a pit.

There are the north’s rulers, all Assyria’s generals, who descended wounded. With their fear and their strength they lay uncircumcised with those wounded by the sword and carried away their torment with those descending to a pit.
King Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all their strength, says the Lord, the Lord.
For I have set his fear upon the land of life, and he will lie among the uncircumcised with those wounded by the sword—Pharaoh and all his multitude—says the Lord, the Lord.”

relationship: close royal mortality ending among worms
rationale: Isaiah sends royal glory into Hades and describes decay and a worm as the king's bedding; Sirach likewise moves from a king dying to the dead person's inheritance of creeping things, beasts and worms.
source_text: Your glory went down to Hades, your abundant gladness. They will spread decay beneath you, and your covering is a worm.

target_units.text: A long illness—the physician mocks it. A king today, and tomorrow he will die.
For when a person dies, he will inherit creeping things, beasts, and worms.

relationship: shared fall-from-heaven image with distinct referents
rationale: Isaiah's taunt, introduced against Babylon's king in 14:4, depicts the dawn-bearer falling from heaven; Jesus describes Satan falling from heaven like lightning. The image is compared without identifying the two figures.
source_text: How the dawn-bearer who rises in the morning fell from heaven! The one dispatching to all the nations was shattered to earth.

target_units.text: He said to them, “I was watching Satan fall from heaven like lightning.

relationship: close proud aspiration to heavenly height among the stars
rationale: Isaiah's speaker plans a throne above heaven's stars; Obadiah likewise rebukes a proud heart imagining a nest among the stars and promises descent to the ground.
source_text: You said in your mind, ‘I will ascend to heaven, set my throne above heaven’s stars, and sit on a high mountain, upon the high mountains toward the north.

target_units.text: The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who camp in holes in the rocks, raising his dwelling high and saying in his heart, “Who will bring me down to the ground?”
If you soar like an eagle, and if you place your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord.

relationship: parallel ruler's aspiration or claim to divine status
rationale: Babylon's king aspires to be like the Most High; Tyre's ruler says he is a god and is reminded that he is human. The claims differ in wording and degree.
source_text: I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’

target_units.text: “And you, son of man, say to the ruler of Tyre: Thus says the Lord: Because your heart was exalted and you said, ‘I am a god; I have inhabited a god’s dwelling in the heart of the sea’—yet you are a human, and not a god, and you made your heart like a god’s heart—

relationship: close reversal from heavenly exaltation to Hades
rationale: Isaiah answers the king's intended ascent with descent to Hades; Jesus similarly contrasts Capernaum's prospective exaltation to heaven with descent to Hades. The addressees are different.
source_text: But now you will descend to Hades and to the earth’s foundations.

target_units.text: And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will descend to Hades! For if the mighty works that occurred in you had occurred in Sodom, it would have remained until today.

relationship: parallel astonishment at Babylon's shattered world power
rationale: Isaiah's observers question the fallen person who provoked the earth and shook kings; Jeremiah likewise exclaims over Babylon, the shattered hammer of the whole earth.
source_text: Those who see you will marvel at you and say, ‘Is this the person who provoked the earth, shook kings,

target_units.text: How the hammer of the whole earth was snapped and shattered! How Babylon became a ruin among nations!

relationship: close refusal to release captives followed by divine intervention
rationale: Isaiah describes the ruler who would not release captives; Jeremiah likewise says Israel and Judah's captors refused to release them and names their strong Redeemer.
source_text: who made the whole inhabited world deserted and pulled down the cities, who did not release those in captivity?’

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Israel’s sons and Judah’s sons have been oppressed together. All who captured them oppressed them, because they did not want to release them.
The One redeeming them is strong; the Lord Almighty is His name. He will judge a case against His adversaries, to remove the land, and He will provoke Babylon’s inhabitants.

relationship: same-chapter contrast between honored royal death and an outcast corpse
rationale: The statement that kings fall asleep in honor, each in his own house, is directly contrasted in the following verse with this ruler thrown out among the dead.
source_text: All the nations’ kings fell asleep in honor, each in his own house;

target_units.text: but you will be thrown into the mountains like an abhorred dead man, with many dead pierced by swords, descending to Hades. As a garment stained with blood will not be clean,

relationship: parallel dishonored disposal of a king's body
rationale: Isaiah's ruler is cast away as an abhorred corpse; Jeremiah similarly denies royal mourning to Jehoiakim and describes his body thrown beyond Jerusalem's gate with a donkey's burial. The kings and locations differ.
source_text: but you will be thrown into the mountains like an abhorred dead man, with many dead pierced by swords, descending to Hades. As a garment stained with blood will not be clean,

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: Woe upon this man! They will certainly not mourn him, O brother! Nor will they weep for him, Alas, lord!
He will be buried with a donkey’s burial; swept up, he will be thrown beyond Jerusalem’s gate.

relationship: close destruction of ungodly offspring
rationale: Isaiah's concluding address denies enduring life to evil offspring; the psalm likewise declares that the ungodly's offspring will be destroyed, contrasting the righteous inheriting the land.
source_text: so neither will you be clean, because you destroyed My land and killed My people. You will certainly not endure for everlasting time, evil offspring.

target_units.text: For the Lord loves judgment and will not abandon His holy ones; they will be guarded for ever. But the lawless will be driven out, and the offspring of the ungodly will be destroyed.
But the righteous will inherit the land and dwell upon it for age upon age.

relationship: related judgment extending ancestral sins to descendants
rationale: Isaiah directs preparing children for slaughter because of the addressee's father's sins; Exodus likewise speaks of fathers' sins repaid upon later generations, specifying those who hate God.
source_text: Prepare your children to be slaughtered because of your father’s sins, so that they do not rise, inherit the earth and fill the earth with cities.”

target_units.text: You shall not bow down to them, neither shall you serve them; for I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, repaying the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate Me,
and showing mercy to thousands, to those who love Me and keep My ordinances.

relationship: contrast with the legal prohibition of death for another generation's sin
rationale: Isaiah's oracle links the children's slaughter with the addressee's father's sins; Deuteronomy forbids sons dying for fathers and assigns death to each person's own sin. The oracle and legal settings differ.
source_text: Prepare your children to be slaughtered because of your father’s sins, so that they do not rise, inherit the earth and fill the earth with cities.”

target_units.text: Fathers shall not die for children, and sons shall not die for fathers. Each shall die for his own sin.

relationship: close removal of offspring, name and remembrance
rationale: Isaiah announces destruction of name, remnant and offspring; the psalm likewise petitions for children destroyed, a name erased and remembrance removed from the earth. The psalm is a petition rather than this divine announcement.
source_text: “I will rise against them,” says the Lord Sabaoth, “and destroy their name, remnant and offspring”—thus says the Lord—

target_units.text: Let his children be destroyed; in one generation let his name be erased.
May his fathers’ lawlessness be remembered before the Lord, and may his mother’s sin not be erased.
Let them be before the Lord continually, and may their memorial be destroyed from the earth,

relationship: parallel ruined imperial capital inhabited by hedgehogs
rationale: Isaiah makes Babylonia deserted with hedgehogs and a muddy abyss; Zephaniah likewise places hedgehogs in ruined Nineveh. Nineveh is described as waterless rather than muddy.
source_text: “and make Babylonia deserted, so that hedgehogs dwell there; she will become nothing. I will make her a muddy abyss for destruction.”

target_units.text: He will stretch His hand against the north and destroy the Assyrian, making Nineveh a waterless wasteland like a wilderness.

Flocks and all the wild animals of the earth will graze within her; chameleons and hedgehogs will lie in her recessed panels. Wild animals will cry in her openings, and ravens in her gateways, for cedar is her structure.

This is the contemptuous city dwelling in confidence, saying in her heart, “I am, and there is no one after me.” How she became a wasteland, pasture for wild animals! Everyone passing through her will hiss and wave his hands.

relationship: close certainty that God's spoken counsel will be accomplished
rationale: Both join God's speech and counsel with their certain accomplishment: what He has planned will stand, and what He has spoken He brings about.
source_text: Thus says the Lord Sabaoth: “As I said, so it will be, and as I counseled, so it will endure,

target_units.text: announcing the last things beforehand, before they came to be—and together they were fulfilled. I said, ‘All My counsel will stand, and I will do everything I have planned,’
calling a bird from the east and from a distant land concerning what I have planned. I spoke and brought it about; I created and acted. I brought him and made his journey prosper.

relationship: narrative counterpart of deliverance from Assyria
rationale: Isaiah promises Assyria's removal and the end of its yoke; the later narrative records Jerusalem's protection, the Assyrian army's destruction and the king's departure and death.
source_text: to destroy the Assyrians from My land and from My mountains. They will become a trampling place; their yoke will be removed from them, and their glory removed from the shoulders.”

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord against the king of the Assyrians: He will certainly not enter this city or shoot a missile against it; he will certainly not bring a shield against it or surround it with a siegework.
By the way he came he will return. Thus says the Lord.
I will shield this city to save it, because of Me and because of David My servant.”
An angel of the Lord went out and killed one hundred eighty-five thousand from the Assyrians’ camp. On rising early in the morning, they found all the bodies dead.
The king of the Assyrians turned back, went away, and lived in Nineveh.
While he was worshiping his cult-image in the house of Nasarach, his sons Adramelech and Sarasar struck him with swords. They escaped safely to Armenia, and his son Asordan reigned in his place.

relationship: parallel divine counsel prevailing over the nations
rationale: Isaiah presents the Lord's counsel and high hand over the world's nations; the psalm likewise contrasts scattered national counsels with the Lord's enduring counsel.
source_text: This is the counsel the Lord has counseled concerning the whole inhabited world, and this the high hand over all the world’s nations.

target_units.text: The Lord scatters the counsels of nations; He nullifies the plans of peoples and nullifies the counsels of rulers.
But the Lord’s counsel remains for ever, the plans of His heart from generation to generation.

relationship: close impossibility of reversing God's action
rationale: Isaiah asks who can turn back God's high hand; the later declaration likewise denies rescue from His hands and asks who can turn back what He does.
source_text: For what the holy God has counseled, who will scatter? And who will turn back the high hand?

target_units.text: still from the beginning. No one rescues from My hands. I will act, and who will turn it back?”

relationship: historical record of the king's death used to date the oracle
rationale: Isaiah dates the utterance to King Achaz's death; Kings records Ahaz's death, burial and succession by Hezekiah. The king's name is rendered differently in the two passages.
source_text: In the year King Achaz died, this utterance came:

target_units.text: Ahaz lay down with his fathers and was buried in David’s city. His son Hezekiah became king in his place.

relationship: parallel warning against rejoicing at an adversary's fall
rationale: Isaiah warns foreigners not to rejoice that their striker's yoke was broken, because dangerous offspring will follow; Proverbs likewise forbids rejoicing at an enemy's fall but gives a different reason.
source_text: “Do not rejoice, all you foreigners, because the yoke of the one striking you was shattered; for from snakes’ seed asp offspring will come, and their offspring will emerge as flying snakes.

target_units.text: If your enemy falls, do not rejoice over him, and at his tripping do not lift yourself up,
for the Lord will see, and it will not please Him, and He will turn His wrath away from him.

relationship: close promise of food for the poor
rationale: Isaiah promises that the poor will be fed and rest in peace; the psalm likewise promises that Zion's poor will be satisfied with loaves. Isaiah also announces famine against the addressees' offspring.
source_text: The poor will be fed through him, and poor men will rest in peace; but he will destroy your seed with famine and destroy your remnant.

target_units.text: I will surely bless her game; I will satisfy her poor with loaves.

relationship: parallel city warning of devastation approaching from the north
rationale: Isaiah summons cities to wail because smoke comes from the north; Jeremiah likewise warns Jerusalem and Benjamin of northern evils and great crushing. The addressed communities differ.
source_text: Wail, gates of cities! Let troubled cities cry out, all the foreigners, because smoke comes from the north, and there is no surviving.

target_units.text: Take courage, sons of Benjamin, from within Jerusalem, and signal with a trumpet in Tekoa, and raise a sign above Beth-haccherem, because evils have looked out from the north, and great crushing is taking place,
and your height will be taken away, daughter of Zion.

relationship: close declaration that God founded Zion
rationale: Isaiah's answer affirms that the Lord founded Zion; the psalm likewise explicitly says that the Most High Himself founded her. Isaiah additionally promises salvation for the humble.
source_text: What will the nations’ kings answer? That the Lord founded Zion, and through Him the humble among the people will be saved.”

target_units.text: “Mother Zion,” a man will say, and a man was born in her; and the Most High Himself founded her.

relationship: parallel oracle of Moab's collapse
rationale: Isaiah announces Moab's country and wall perishing in a night; Jeremiah likewise announces the loss of Moab's cities and Moab's shattering, without that overnight timing.
source_text: The utterance against Moab’s country. In a night Moab’s country will perish, for in a night the wall of Moab’s country will perish.

target_units.text: For Moab, thus said the Lord: Woe to Nebo, for she perished! Kiriathaim was taken; Amath was disgraced and defeated.
There is no longer healing for Moab, a boast in Heshbon. They devised evils against her: We cut her off from a nation, and she will certainly cease. A sword will walk behind you.
For a sound of people crying out comes from Horonaim: destruction and great shattering!
Moab was shattered; announce it in Zogora.

relationship: close announcement of Dibon's devastation
rationale: Isaiah says Debon too will perish; Jeremiah addresses resident Dibon with descent from glory, crushing and ruined fortification. Both locate this within Moab's judgment.
source_text: Grieve over yourselves, for Debon too will perish. Where your altar is, there you will go up to weep. Over Nabau of Moab’s country, wail: baldness upon every head, every arm cut.

target_units.text: Come down from glory and sit in dampness, resident Dibon. Be crushed, for Moab perished; he came up against you, ruining your fortification.

relationship: close bodily mourning throughout Moab
rationale: Both describe baldness or shaving upon every head during Moab's mourning. Isaiah additionally names cut arms; Jeremiah names shaved beards, beating hands and sackcloth.
source_text: Grieve over yourselves, for Debon too will perish. Where your altar is, there you will go up to weep. Over Nabau of Moab’s country, wail: baldness upon every head, every arm cut.

target_units.text: They will shave every head in every place; every beard will be shaved, all hands will beat themselves, and on every waist is sackcloth.

relationship: close mourning upon Moab's rooftops and squares
rationale: Isaiah places sackcloth and lament in squares, roofs and lanes; Jeremiah likewise combines sackcloth and beating hands with Moab's rooftops and squares.
source_text: In her squares put on sackcloth and beat yourselves in mourning; upon her roofs and in her lanes all of you wail with weeping.

target_units.text: They will shave every head in every place; every beard will be shaved, all hands will beat themselves, and on every waist is sackcloth.
And on all Moab’s rooftops and in her squares—for I shattered Moab, says the Lord, like a vessel for which there is no use.

relationship: close cries from Heshbon and Elealeh
rationale: Both Moab oracles place cries at the cities rendered Hesebon/Heshbon and Eleale/Elealeh. Isaiah also says the voice reaches Iassa, which this Jeremiah unit does not name.
source_text: For Hesebon and Eleale have cried out; their voice was heard as far as Iassa. Therefore Moab’s loins cry out; her soul will know.

target_units.text: From Heshbon’s cry as far as Elealeh, their cities raised their voice; from Zogor to Horonaim and Aglath-salisia, for even Nebrim’s water will become a burning.

relationship: close Moabite road imagery of weeping and shattering
rationale: Both describe upward movement with weeping and a road marked by a cry of destruction. Isaiah names Louith and Aroniim; Jeremiah names Alaoth and Horonaim in its comparable description.
source_text: Moab’s heart cries within her as far as Segor, for she is a three-year-old heifer. On Louith’s ascent they will go up toward you weeping; along Aroniim’s road destruction and shaking cry out.

target_units.text: For Alaoth was filled with weeping; he will go up weeping on Horonaim’s road. You heard a cry of shattering:

relationship: related devastation of named Moabite waters
rationale: Isaiah names Nemrim's deserted water and vanished grass; Jeremiah names Nebrim's water becoming a burning. Both set these waters within Moab's devastation, with different stated effects.
source_text: Nemrim’s water will be deserted, and her grass cease; for there will be no green grass.

target_units.text: From Heshbon’s cry as far as Elealeh, their cities raised their voice; from Zogor to Horonaim and Aglath-salisia, for even Nebrim’s water will become a burning.

relationship: contrast between predicted blood-filled water and water mistaken for blood
rationale: Isaiah announces Remmon's water filled with blood; Kings describes Moab seeing fiery-red water like blood and wrongly concluding that the opposing kings killed one another. The events are not identified.
source_text: Remmon’s water will fill with blood; for I will bring Arabs upon Remmon and remove Moab’s offspring, Ariel and Adama’s remainder.

target_units.text: They rose early in the morning, and the sun rose over the waters. From opposite them Moab saw the waters fiery red, like blood.
They said, ‘This is blood from the sword! The kings have fought and each has struck his neighbor. Now, Moab, to the spoils!’
They entered Israel’s camp. Israel rose and struck Moab, and they fled before them. They kept going in and striking Moab.

relationship: related bird imagery for Moab's displacement
rationale: Isaiah compares daughter Moab with a fledgling removed from a flying bird; Jeremiah describes Moab's people leaving cities and becoming like doves nesting among rocks. The bird situations differ.
source_text: For you will be like a fledgling removed from a bird taking flight, Daughter Moab. Then, Arnon,

target_units.text: Moab’s inhabitants left the cities and lived among rocks. They became like doves nesting among rocks at a pit’s mouth.

relationship: shared conjunction of midday darkness and mourning
rationale: Isaiah places flight in midday darkness beside the command for a shelter of mourning; Amos likewise joins daylight darkening at midday with mourning and lament. Amos expressly attributes the darkening to God.
